rationale: Isaiah announces Damascus's removal as a city and its ruin. Kings records the Assyrian capture and deportation of Damascus and the killing of its king, supplying a concrete narrative counterpart to the city's downfall.

Isaiah pictures the abandoned city as a resting place for flocks. Zephaniah similarly turns Nineveh from a confident city into a wasteland where flocks and wild animals dwell; the cities differ, but their urban desolation becomes animal pasture in both descriptions.

Isaiah says Damascus will lose its kingdom and the Syrian remainder will perish. Kings records Damascus's capture and the death of Raasson, matching the removal of the city's royal power without supplying every detail of Isaiah's oracle.

Isaiah includes the loss of Ephraim's defensive refuge alongside Damascus's downfall. Kings describes Samaria's siege, capture and Israel's deportation, a narrative counterpart concerning the northern kingdom's lost security.

Isaiah announces the failure of Jacob's glory and the shaking of its abundance. Hosea likewise answers the people's increased sin by turning their glory into dishonor; both describe the reversal of Israel's former distinction.

The stripping of a standing harvest in Isaiah 17:5 introduces the small remainder described in the following verse. Isaiah 24:13 likewise pictures judgment among the nations through olive gleaning and the end of grape harvest, using agricultural removal to portray diminished populations.

Isaiah 17 specifies the few olive berries left on high branches after gathering. Isaiah 24 again uses the gleaning of an olive tree and a finished grape harvest for what remains among the nations; both passages make the remnant visible through the same harvesting image.

Isaiah 17 anticipates people looking to their Maker and Israel's Holy One. Isaiah 31 condemns those who trust Egypt's horses and chariots instead of that same Holy One, contrasting the restored allegiance with the misplaced reliance.

Isaiah 17 anticipates abandoning trust in altars and objects made by hands and fingers. Isaiah 2 describes the earlier condition in which the land was filled with handmade abominations and people bowed before what their fingers made.

Isaiah 17 describes people ceasing to regard handmade altars, trees and abominations as objects of trust. Isaiah 27 connects Jacob's sin being removed with altar stones reduced to dust and trees and idols cut down, giving a corresponding picture of idolatry's removal.

Isaiah expressly compares the coming abandonment of cities with the Amorites and Hivites yielding before Israel. Joshua names those peoples among Israel's opponents and recalls God delivering their cities and land to Israel.

Isaiah explains the disaster by the people abandoning God their Savior and forgetting their Helper. Deuteronomy's song likewise says Jacob forsook God his Maker and Savior and forgot the God who nourished him.

Isaiah joins the roar and disturbance of many nations with surging water. The Psalm also places troubled nations beside the sea's hollow and the sound of its waves; the connection is this shared juxtaposition, without claiming that either text describes the same event.

Isaiah's nations are pursued like windblown chaff and wheel-dust carried by a squall. The Psalm asks God to make hostile rulers like a wheel and straw before wind and pursue them with His storm, closely matching the combined images of pursuit and wind-driven debris.

Isaiah places mourning toward evening and its disappearance before morning within a pronouncement concerning plunderers. Kings records the Assyrian army being struck at night and its dead discovered early in the morning, illustrating a sudden overnight reversal without identifying it as the oracle's sole possible referent.

Isaiah 18 describes a mountain signal and an audible trumpet in its picture of an inhabited land. Isaiah 11 raises a signal to the nations to gather dispersed Israel and Judah; both use a conspicuous public signal within a prophecy concerning peoples and their land.

Isaiah 18 associates security in God's city with midday light and a dew cloud at harvest. Isaiah 4 portrays Zion shaded by cloud and sheltered from heat and harsh weather, linking the city's divine protection with atmospheric imagery.

Isaiah pictures sickles cutting off grape growth before the harvest ripens. Joel commands sickles at the vintage as the nations' evils multiply. Both use cutting and gathering a vineyard for judgment, while the premature removal in Isaiah differs from Joel's full winepress.

Isaiah leaves the cut-down subject to heaven's birds and the earth's wild beasts. Jeremiah explicitly gives the people's dead as food to those same two groups, presenting a corresponding image of exposed remains after judgment.

Isaiah anticipates gifts reaching the Lord at Zion from the people associated with Ethiopia's rivers. Zephaniah likewise anticipates sacrifices brought to God from the far reaches of those rivers, joining the same distant region with worship offered to Him.

Isaiah brings distant people's gifts to the place of the Lord's name on Mount Zion. The Psalm links gifts at God's Jerusalem sanctuary with envoys from Egypt and Ethiopia hastening its hand toward God, placing foreign approach and worship in the same setting.

Isaiah's vision has the Lord enter Egypt and its handmade objects shake before Him. Exodus records the Lord passing through Egypt and executing vengeance against its gods; both portray His intervention as exposing the impotence of Egypt's objects of worship.

Isaiah depicts the Lord coming to Egypt upon a light cloud. The Psalm depicts God's descent and flight with darkness and cloud around Him. The shared connection is heavenly weather surrounding His powerful arrival, not identical vehicles or destinations.

Isaiah 19 sets Egyptians against brothers, neighbors, cities and districts within Egypt. Isaiah 9 pictures Manasseh and Ephraim consuming one another even while joining against Judah; both portray internal conflict as part of a nation's judgment.

The troubled Egyptians turn to statues, speakers from the earth and belly-speakers. Isaiah 8 names the same kinds of speakers and contrasts consulting them with a nation's turning to its God, clarifying the misplaced religious recourse.

Isaiah announces Egypt's delivery into harsh human rule without naming the masters. Ezekiel explicitly gives Egypt and its wealth to Nebuchadnezzar as his army's wages; both present foreign domination as divinely permitted judgment, without equating all of Isaiah's unnamed rulers with one king.

Isaiah announces the Egyptian river's failure and drying. Ezekiel's Egypt oracle likewise makes the rivers desolate as the country is destroyed, connecting the judgment of Egypt with the collapse of its river system.

Isaiah extends the water failure to rivers, canals and marshes. Ezekiel likewise includes Egypt's desolate rivers in the destruction of the land and what fills it; the comparison concerns the damaged water system, not a claim that Ezekiel names every plant in Isaiah.

Isaiah's riverbank growth and sown crops dry up and perish. Joel likewise describes failed grain, a dried vine and dried field trees, connecting judgment with the disappearance of agricultural abundance.

Isaiah's failing river leaves hook-and-net fishers mourning. Ezekiel's healing river produces abundant fish and places for fishers and their nets, providing a specific contrast between devastated and restored fishing livelihoods.

Isaiah names the shame of Egypt's flax and fine-linen workers. Ezekiel identifies embroidered fine linen from Egypt among Tyre's valuable furnishings, showing the particular Egyptian textile trade whose workers Isaiah places under judgment.

Isaiah 19 calls Tanis's rulers fools and exposes the king's wise counselors' foolish counsel. Isaiah 29 similarly announces the destruction of the wise people's wisdom and concealment of the discerning people's understanding under divine judgment.

Egypt's wise men are challenged to announce what the Lord has counseled against their nation. Isaiah 44 describes God turning the discerning backward and making their counsel foolish, likewise exposing the limits of human wisdom before the Lord's own counsel.

Isaiah names the failure of Tanis's rulers and the misguidance associated with Memphis's rulers. Ezekiel's Egypt oracle likewise targets Memphis's magnates and announces fire upon Tanis, connecting the same Egyptian centers with judgment on their power.

Isaiah 19 likens Egypt's confused guidance to a drunken person's wandering. Isaiah 28 describes priest and prophet wandering and losing their senses through wine and sikera; both use intoxication to depict those who should guide others becoming unreliable.

Isaiah 19 denies Egypt productive work from head to tail and beginning to end. Isaiah 9 also uses head and tail for a judgment extending through the people's leadership, identifying elders and false prophets; the repeated image expresses comprehensive failure rather than a literal anatomical action.

Isaiah describes Egypt trembling before the Lord's hand through the ancient battle image of being like women. Nahum uses the same image for Nineveh's people as its gates open to enemies. The connection records the two texts' portrayal of military vulnerability.

Isaiah says the naming of Judah will terrify Egypt because of the Lord's counsel. The Exodus song likewise describes other nations hearing and trembling before the strength of God's arm as His people approach; both connect foreign fear with divine action or counsel, though the nations and occasions differ.

Isaiah's Egyptian cities speak the Canaanite language and swear by the Lord's name. Zephaniah joins changed speech among peoples with calling upon that name and serving Him, linking a linguistic change with renewed religious allegiance without identifying City-Asedek.

Isaiah places an altar and a border pillar for the Lord within Egypt, called a sign in the following verse. Joshua's border dispute is answered by an altar serving as a witness to shared belonging to the Lord. Joshua expressly excludes sacrificial use for that witness altar, so the comparison concerns public testimony rather than identical ritual rules.

Egypt cries to the Lord because of oppressors, and He sends a man who saves by judging. Judges likewise has Israel cry out and receive Othniel as a savior who judges and delivers, making Egypt's promised rescue resemble Israel's earlier deliverance pattern.

Isaiah anticipates Egyptians knowing the Lord and offering worship to Him. Zechariah includes Egypt among the nations accountable to come and worship the Lord at Jerusalem, with a warning for refusal; both expressly place Egypt within the sphere of worship of Israel's God.

Isaiah joins God's striking Egypt with healing, Egypt's return and His answering them. Hosea likewise calls for return to the Lord because the One who strikes will heal and restore, sharing the sequence of discipline, return and restoration.

Isaiah 19 opens a road between Egypt and Assyria. Isaiah 11 promises a passage for God's remaining people in Egypt, compared with the exodus. Both visions associate Egypt with renewed movement through a divinely announced passage; Isaiah 11:16 does not itself name the Assyrian end of the road.

Isaiah places Israel alongside Egypt and Assyria in blessing upon the earth. God's promise to Abram similarly extends blessing beyond his own household to all the earth's tribes, supplying a broader covenantal setting for the blessing of these named foreign peoples.

Isaiah calls people in Egypt and among the Assyrians God's people while retaining Israel as His inheritance. Romans discusses calling both Jews and Gentiles and cites the declaration that former outsiders become My people. The comparison concerns God's people-language in these differing settings: Romans explicitly names Jews and Gentiles, whereas Isaiah names people in Egypt and among the Assyrians.

Isaiah obeys a command to remove his sackcloth and sandals as part of a warning about captivity. Ezekiel is commanded to depict and enact a city's siege as a sign for Israel. In both, a commanded visible act conveys a coming national disaster; the actions and recipients differ.

God explicitly makes Isaiah's unusual appearance a sign for Egypt and Ethiopia. Ezekiel is likewise called a portent whose conduct anticipates what the people will experience, sharing the function of a prophet's lived action as warning.

Isaiah 20 portrays Egypt's and Ethiopia's captives led away exposed and without sandals. Isaiah 47 orders Babylon to uncover herself and announces visible shame, using bodily exposure for the humiliation of another powerful nation under judgment.

Egypt is ashamed when Ethiopia, its trusted glory, fails. Isaiah 30 likewise says reliance on Egypt will yield shame instead of assistance. The countries occupy different positions in the two warnings, but both expose the disgrace of a foreign protector that cannot deliver.

Isaiah 20's island residents see that their hoped-for refuge cannot escape Assyria and question their own safety. Isaiah 31 condemns dependence on Egyptian military help and says helpers and helped will fail together, explaining the vulnerability of such borrowed security.

Isaiah introduces a frightening vision through a squall coming across the wilderness. Jeremiah likewise describes an approaching enemy and his chariots as cloud and storm, sharing the imagery of a destructive force sweeping in upon its hearers.

Isaiah's harsh vision names Elamites and Persian envoys before announcing Babylon's fall in verse 9. Daniel records the Chaldean kingship passing to the Medes and Persians. The connection is the Persian presence within the downfall of Babylon, not an identification of every figure in Isaiah's vision.

Isaiah 21 describes the seer's weakness and labor pains like a woman giving birth. Isaiah 13 uses the same birth-pain comparison for those troubled by the Lord's approaching judgment, portraying overwhelming distress through the same bodily image.

Isaiah's heart wanders and his soul stands in fear within the harsh vision. Jeremiah likewise describes his raging soul and torn heart as he hears war and the land's crushing, giving a corresponding account of a prophet's inward anguish over announced disaster.

Isaiah's Babylon vision places eating and drinking beside a summons to rulers to prepare shields. Daniel's account likewise begins with Babylon's king and companions banqueting before the kingdom's loss. This connects the settings of feasting under impending overthrow without asserting that Isaiah identifies Daniel's particular banquet.

Isaiah is told to station a watcher and report what is seen. Habakkuk likewise takes a watch position to receive God's response and is told to write the vision clearly, joining vigilance with the communication of revelation.

The watcher's sight of mounted riders and two horsemen is followed by the appearance of a rider with a two-horse team and the announcement of Babylon's fall. The repeated mounted figure connects the vision's observed sign with its reported message.

Isaiah's watcher describes remaining at his post by day and through the night. Habakkuk similarly stands at his watch and is instructed to wait for the vision's appointed arrival, sharing persistent attentiveness rather than immediate visible fulfillment.

Isaiah's report announces that Babylon has fallen and its handmade objects have been shattered. Jeremiah likewise proclaims that Babylon suddenly fell and was shattered. The retained connection is the explicit announcement of the same city's collapse; Jeremiah's verse does not repeat Isaiah's detail about statues.

Isaiah addresses those who remain and suffer, asking them to hear God's announcement after the report of Babylon's fall. Isaiah 48 expressly addresses flight from Babylon and proclaims that the Lord rescued Jacob, giving a related message of deliverance to those affected by Babylon's power.

The Idumea vision begins with a call from Seir to guard the battlements. Earlier in the chapter a watcher is stationed and commanded to report, so the repeated watch commission provides a literary link between these distinct prophetic scenes without treating their locations as identical.

The answer in the Idumea vision speaks of watching morning and night. The earlier watcher likewise stands continually by day and through the night, repeating the motif of sustained vigilance across the chapter's scenes.

Isaiah 21 calls for water for the thirsty and loaves for fugitives. Isaiah 58 similarly commands sharing bread with the hungry and bringing homeless poor people into one's house, making material aid to displaced and needy people the specific point of comparison.

Isaiah describes people fleeing the sword, ready arrows and the casualties of war. Jeremiah pictures inhabitants abandoning towns and seeking hiding places at the sound of a horseman and drawn bow, describing the same concrete effect of armed attack on people's flight.

Isaiah 21 gives Kedar one year measured like a hired worker's year before its glory fails. Isaiah 16 uses the same hired-worker measure for three years before Moab's glory is dishonored. The repeated formula is explicit, while the peoples and durations remain distinct.

Isaiah reduces the remaining arrows of Kedar's strong sons to a few. Jeremiah calls for Elam's bow, described as the beginning of its dominion, to be shattered, likewise expressing a foreign nation's loss of power through the defeat of its archery; the two nations are not identified with each other.

Isaiah portrays Jerusalem's rulers fleeing and captives being harshly bound. Kings later records the king's flight from besieged Jerusalem, pursuit, capture and binding with fetters, providing a concrete narrative parallel without establishing that every detail of the oracle concerns that one siege.

Isaiah insists on bitter weeping over the shattering of the daughter of his people. Lamentations likewise joins tears and inward anguish to the shattering of the daughter of the people, sharing both the personified community and the reason for the lament.

Isaiah announces a day of destruction and trampling from the Lord in Zion's ravine. Lamentations describes the Lord setting a time to crush the city's strong men and treading a winepress for Daughter Judah, sharing the portrayal of Jerusalem's humiliation under divine judgment.

Isaiah identifies Elamites with quivers in the assembled battle force. Jeremiah likewise identifies Elam's bow as an expression of its dominion, providing a specific correspondence between the named people and its military archery rather than equating the two campaigns.

Isaiah pictures Jerusalem's ravines filled with chariots and its gates blocked by horsemen. Kings describes Babylon's force encircling and besieging Jerusalem, providing a narrative counterpart to the city's military enclosure without claiming that Kings specifies Isaiah's chariots.

Isaiah's view of David's citadel includes water from the old pool diverted into the city. Chronicles records Hezekiah blocking the upper outlet of Gihon and directing its waters toward the City of David, a specific narrative parallel concerning the city's redirected water supply.

Isaiah says Jerusalem's houses were pulled down to fortify its wall. Jeremiah likewise names the city's houses and royal houses torn down for siegeworks and defenses, matching the conversion of domestic buildings into defensive materials.

Isaiah condemns arranging water between the walls while ignoring the city's Maker. Chronicles also describes water measures and wall-building against a siege, but explicitly urges trust in the Lord rather than arms of flesh. The comparison distinguishes the engineering measures from the reliance placed upon them.

Isaiah says the Lord called for weeping, lamentation and sackcloth. Joel likewise calls for return to God with fasting, weeping and mourning, adding that the heart rather than merely garments should be torn; both address the response sought when judgment approaches.

Isaiah's revelers say, Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die, instead of answering the call to mourn. Paul repeats that sentence while testing the consequences of denying resurrection, using the same expression of immediate gratification under death's horizon.

Isaiah announces that this sin will not be forgiven before the offenders die. Samuel receives an oath that Eli's household wrongdoing will never be expiated by incense or sacrifices. Both give a solemn sentence that ordinary expectation of expiation cannot cancel, while their wording and scope differ.

Isaiah addresses Somnas as treasurer before announcing the transfer of stewardship to Eliakim. Kings places Somnas as scribe beside Eliakim son of Chelkias, the steward, preserving the two named officials while distinguishing the offices reported in the two passages.

Isaiah challenges Somnas over the memorial he quarried for himself and his rock-cut dwelling. Matthew likewise describes Joseph's own tomb cut in rock. The physical parallel concerns a self-prepared rock-cut memorial and Joseph's own rock-cut tomb, preserving their distinct terms; Isaiah's criticism of Somnas is not transferred to Joseph.
The Lord's removal of the official's robe in verse 17 is answered by Eliakim being clothed in that robe in verse 21. The repeated garment makes the transfer of office visible within the same oracle.

Isaiah threatens the addressed official with removal to a distant country where he will die and lose his honor. Jeremiah likewise tells an official and his household that they will go captive and that he will die and be buried in Babylon, sharing the personal sentence of exile and death abroad.

The removal of the present official from his stewardship is matched by the placing of that stewardship in Eliakim's hands. The two verses express the loss and grant of the same authority within the oracle.
Isaiah names the incoming servant as Eliakim son of Chelkias. Kings names Eliakim with the same father and identifies him as steward, providing a precise personal and official correspondence.

Eliakim's stewardship will make him like a father to Jerusalem and Judah's inhabitants. Joseph likewise describes God making him as a father to Pharaoh and ruler over Egypt. Both use paternal language for divinely appointed civil responsibility rather than biological parenthood.

Isaiah grants the stewardship to the Eliakim named in the preceding verse. Kings explicitly identifies Eliakim son of Chelkias as steward. The correspondence verifies the named office, without claiming that Kings repeats the robe, crown or paternal imagery.

Verse 23 establishes the ruler in a trustworthy place and promises a throne of glory. Verse 25 repeats the trustworthy-place description but announces shaking, falling and removal of the attached glory, creating an explicit reversal within the oracle.

The household's glorious people trust in and hang upon the appointed figure. The following judgment removes the glory upon that figure as he falls, connecting the dependents' reliance with the vulnerability of the office supporting them.

The person established in a trustworthy place is now shaken and falls. The earlier verse uses that same establishment language for the ruler's promised position and glory, so the ending must be read against the security announced there.

Isaiah calls Carthage's ships to wail over Tyre's destruction and captivity. Ezekiel places Carthaginian traders among Tyre's maritime company and depicts that company's catastrophic fall in the sea. Both connect Tyre's collapse with the shipping network that depended on her.

Isaiah addresses Phoenician island traders crossing the sea. Ezekiel names Sidon, Arvad and Byblos within Tyre's network of rowers, pilots and advisers, with ships coming across the sea. The target supplies a concrete portrait of the coastal maritime community addressed by Isaiah.

Isaiah compares the nations' traders to a harvest being brought in. Ezekiel describes Tyre's abundant sea commerce filling nations and enriching their kings. Both portray the gathering and abundance of international trade; Isaiah's harvest comparison is not treated as a statement specifically about Egyptian grain.

Isaiah says news concerning Tyre will bring pain to Egypt. Ezekiel's lament describes island inhabitants becoming gloomy and their kings weeping over Tyre. The affected regions differ, but both oracles portray Tyre's downfall causing grief beyond the city itself.

The call to wail addresses island residents being sent toward Carthage, repeating the opening appeal to Carthage's ships. The recurrence extends the lament over Tyre from the ships named at the oracle's opening to the island community now addressed.

Isaiah recalls Tyre's longstanding insolence before she was handed over. Ezekiel exposes her ruler's exalted heart, divine pretensions and pride in wealth gained through trade. The target concentrates in the ruler the commercial city's arrogance condemned by Isaiah.

Isaiah describes Tyre's merchants as glorious rulers of the earth while asking who planned these things against her. Ezekiel says her commerce enriched all the earth's kings. Both explain the extraordinary international influence of Tyre through the wealth of her merchants.

The Lord plans Tyre's humiliation to dissolve the insolence of the glorious and dishonor earthly glory. Isaiah 2 likewise announces the humbling of human height, proud people, towers and splendid ships so that the Lord alone is exalted. Tyre's judgment fits this wider pattern of overturned human grandeur.

Isaiah tells the inhabitants to work their land because ships no longer arrive from Carthage. Ezekiel's maritime lament includes Carthaginian traders before the ship-like city's shattering and the fall of its company. Both describe the collapse of sea commerce; Ezekiel does not give Isaiah's instruction about farming.

Isaiah attributes the loss of strength at sea to the Lord's command against Canaan's power. Zechariah names Tyre and Sidon, then announces the Lord's striking Tyre's strength into the sea despite her fortifications and wealth. Both make divine judgment decisive over the coast's maritime strength.

Isaiah warns that even flight to the Kitians will bring no rest. Deuteronomy likewise describes scattered people finding no rest among foreign nations. The shared condition is refuge failing to provide security; the covenant warning addresses Israel, whereas Isaiah's immediate oracle concerns the coastal population.

The warning of no rest in the Chaldeans' devastated land repeats the preceding warning of no rest among the Kitians. Repeating the same outcome for two possible destinations closes off the expectation that another foreign refuge will escape the announced calamity.

Isaiah commands Carthage's ships to wail because their fortress has perished. Ezekiel portrays rowers leaving their ships, maritime people standing ashore and raising a bitter cry, followed by a lament over Tyre. Both turn the trading fleet into mourners for the fallen city.

Isaiah assigns Tyre seventy years of being left before her condition changes. Jeremiah also marks a period of national humiliation and service by seventy years, followed by divine action. The shared bounded duration is explicit, but the two passages concern different subjects and do not establish an identical chronology.

Isaiah promises that Tyre will return to her former state as a trading center for the world's kingdoms. Ezekiel identifies Tyre as the sea's entrance and trading place for peoples from many islands. That portrait makes concrete the international commercial role Isaiah says will be restored.

relationship: foreign wealth consecrated to the Lord
rationale: Isaiah dedicates Tyre's trade and wages to the Lord and to the support of those dwelling before Him. Isaiah 60 likewise brings sea and national wealth toward Zion, culminating in acceptable offerings and the glorification of God's house. Both redirect international prosperity toward the Lord's service.

Isaiah announces the Lord's devastation of the inhabited world and scattering of its residents. Zephaniah similarly announces the removal of humanity and other creatures from the earth's face. Both use comprehensive earthly destruction to introduce divine judgment, without restricting Isaiah's statement to one named city.

Isaiah places people and priest under the same impending condition before listing other social pairs. Hosea likewise says the people will be like the priest in a sentence of recompense. Both remove the expectation that priestly position exempts someone from the people's judgment.

Isaiah says buyer and seller will share the same condition when judgment comes. Ezekiel warns the buyer not to rejoice and the seller not to lament when the appointed day arrives, because ordinary exchange no longer offers security. Both suspend the usual contrast between commercial gain and loss.

Isaiah grounds the earth's destruction in what the Lord's mouth has spoken. Peter similarly places the present world under a judgment reserved by God's word, recalling the earlier world's destruction by water. The connection is divine speech and world judgment; Peter specifies water and fire, which this Isaiah unit does not.

Isaiah describes the earth and its high inhabitants mourning under devastation. Hosea likewise makes the land mourn and diminish together with its inhabitants because of their offenses. Both present the land as participating in the consequences of human wrongdoing.

Isaiah explains the earth's lawlessness through transgressed law and changed ordinances and covenant. Leviticus connects refusal of God's judgments and commandments, dissolving His covenant, with ensuing distress. The shared covenantal pattern is explicit, while Isaiah's wider earthly scope is not reduced to every detail of Leviticus's penalties.

Isaiah says a curse follows the inhabitants' sin and leaves few people. Deuteronomy likewise warns that disobedience will leave the formerly numerous people few in number. Both connect culpable refusal of God with the drastic reduction of a population.

Isaiah makes wine and vine mourn while those who bring gladness groan. Joel likewise describes ruined agricultural produce and a dried vine, saying human beings have put joy to shame. Both join vine and wine imagery with troubled human gladness, while Joel's stated causal wording is preserved.

Isaiah lists the end of tambourine joy and the lyre's sound among judgment's effects. Ezekiel's sentence upon Tyre likewise ends its musicians and the audible sound of psalteries. The shared image is a formerly festive community made musically silent by destruction.

Isaiah describes every city deserted and a house shut against entry. Jeremiah similarly depicts inhabitants fleeing at the sound of horseman and bow until every city is abandoned and no one dwells in them. Both portray judgment through empty urban habitation, though Jeremiah names the immediate military cause.

Isaiah commands lament over wine because the earth's gladness has ceased. Joel calls wine drinkers to weep and lament because gladness and joy have been removed from their mouths. The combination of wine, commanded mourning and lost joy makes the correspondence specific.

Isaiah 24 leaves cities deserted and abandoned houses perishing. The answer to Isaiah's earlier question about duration likewise describes cities without inhabitants, houses without people and a desolate land. Both define the severity of judgment through the disappearance of settled human life.

Isaiah 24 compares the nations under judgment to an olive tree gleaned after harvest. Isaiah 17 spells out the same image as a few berries remaining on high branches. The earlier description clarifies how a gleaned tree can portray the small remainder after devastation.

Those left on the earth rejoice with the Lord's glory in Isaiah 24. Isaiah 12 calls Zion's inhabitants to sing, announce His glorious deeds and rejoice because Israel's Holy One is exalted among them. Both place communal praise of the Lord's glory within a setting of salvation after distress.

Isaiah 24 places the Lord's glory and glorious name in the sea's islands. Isaiah 42 explicitly summons islands, sea travelers and distant inhabitants to glorify His name and announce His deeds. Both extend the Lord's praise beyond the land to maritime peoples.

relationship: contrasting destinies of the devout and impious
rationale: Isaiah's report couples hope for the devout with woe for rejecters of the law. Proverbs likewise preserves hope for the righteous while the impious person's boast perishes. Both contrast hope for the righteous with calamity for the ungodly; Proverbs specifically frames its contrast at death.

Isaiah announces fear, pit and trap upon the earth's inhabitant. Jeremiah uses the same three dangers, in a different order, against resident Moab. The tightly shared formulation depicts inescapable danger, while the addressed population differs.

Both passages say that fleeing fear leads into a pit and climbing from the pit leads into a trap. Jeremiah directs the sequence against Moab in her visitation year, whereas Isaiah places it within upheaval of earth and heaven. The successive failed escapes are a close verbal and structural parallel.

Isaiah connects the failed escapes with heaven's opened windows and shaken earthly foundations. Genesis describes the opening of heaven's floodgates when the flood begins. Both use openings above as a sign of catastrophic judgment; Isaiah's unit is not thereby identified as a second narration of Noah's flood.

Isaiah describes the earth utterly agitated and at a loss. Hebrews discusses God's shaking of earth and heaven and the removal of created things that can be shaken. Both make shaking an image of the created order's inability to remain secure before divine action; no direct quotation of this Isaiah verse is claimed.

Isaiah pictures the earth tilting and shaking before an irreversible fall under lawlessness. The psalm also speaks of God shaking and fracturing the earth, but pleads for its healing. The shared physical image supports the comparison while the plea for repair and announced final collapse remain distinct.

Isaiah 24 directs God's hand against heaven's array as well as earthly kings. Isaiah 34 depicts heaven rolling up and its stars falling. Both extend the imagery of divine judgment to the heavenly order, without requiring a particular identification of the array with named spiritual beings.

Isaiah describes confinement in a fortress and prison followed much later by visitation. Peter describes sinful angels confined in gloom and kept for judgment. Both present restraint before subsequent divine reckoning; Isaiah's visitation is not called release, and its prisoners are not equated with Peter's angels.

Isaiah says the Lord will reign in Zion and Jerusalem and be glorified before the elders. Micah likewise promises that the Lord will reign over the gathered remnant on Mount Zion. Both place the Lord's rule on Zion beyond the surrounding scenes of affliction and judgment.

Isaiah promises to glorify God and sing His name because He has done wondrous things. The psalm likewise calls for a new song because the Lord has done wonders and worked salvation. In both, accomplished divine wonders are the stated reason for singing praise.

Isaiah's praise names God's wondrous action as an ancient, true plan. Isaiah 46 declares that God's counsel will stand and that He will do all He has planned, announcing outcomes before they happen. Both connect trustworthy divine planning with events brought to completion.

Isaiah celebrates the reduction of fortified cities and says the ungodly city will never be rebuilt. Ezekiel similarly pronounces that Tyre will become bare rock and will not be rebuilt. The shared feature is irreversible urban ruin; Isaiah's unnamed city is not identified as Tyre solely from that resemblance.

Isaiah says poor people and wronged communities will bless God. The psalm calls the poor to rejoice because the Lord hears the needy and does not despise His bound ones. Both make the response of the disadvantaged central to praise for divine help.

Isaiah calls God a helper and shelter for lowly, needy and wronged people. The psalm likewise names the Lord a refuge for the needy and helper in distress. The correspondence concerns God's particular protection of the vulnerable rather than an unspecified claim of help.

Isaiah portrays fainthearted, thirsty people blessing God amid oppression, following the promise of His shelter. The psalm recounts hungry, thirsty people whose strength fails, their cry and rescue, and a call to acknowledge God's mercies. Both bring thanksgiving out of the distress pictured through thirst and weakness.

Isaiah promises gladness and wine for all nations on the Lord's mountain. Jesus speaks of many arriving from east and west to recline with the patriarchs in the kingdom. Both envision people beyond a single local community sharing a celebratory divine welcome; Isaiah's native wording about wine and perfume is preserved.

Isaiah says the plan on this mountain concerns all nations. Isaiah 2 likewise gathers nations to the Lord's mountain for His instruction and judgment. The connection is the mountain as the setting of God's purpose for the nations; this source unit is not described as mentioning a veil or shroud.

Isaiah 25 says God removes every tear from every face and takes away His people's reproach. Isaiah 65 likewise promises that weeping and crying will no longer be heard in the restored Jerusalem. Both describe the removal of communal sorrow by God, without altering Isaiah 25's distinctive preceding statement about death.

Isaiah's people recognize their God and rejoice in the salvation for which they hoped. The psalm calls for rejoicing in the Lord's day, cries for salvation and acknowledges that the Lord God has shone upon His people. Both join communal joy, divine recognition and salvation in worship.

Isaiah compares Moab's trampling to the treading of a threshing floor. Micah gathers hostile nations like sheaves and commands Zion to thresh them. Both employ the crushing action of threshing to picture defeat of hostile peoples, while their named agents and immediate targets differ.

Within the oracle against Moab, Isaiah 25 announces the bringing down of insolence. Isaiah 16 likewise names Moab's excessive insolence and arrogance before its country-wide lament. Both connect Moab's humiliation with the pride that preceded it.

Isaiah 25 brings the height of the wall's refuge down to the ground. The following song likewise says God brings down those dwelling high and casts fortified cities to the ground. The repeated movement from elevated defenses to ground level links the adjoining judgment descriptions.

Isaiah 26 makes salvation a wall and encircling wall for the fortified city. Isaiah 60 similarly names the restored city's walls Salvation. Both portray the community's saving security through city defenses, rather than treating physical fortification alone as the source of safety.

Isaiah commands the gates to open for a people keeping righteousness and truth. The psalm asks for the gates of righteousness to open and declares that the righteous enter the Lord's gate. Both connect admission through the gates with the character of the entering worshipers.

Isaiah describes people holding truth and keeping peace, with their hope in God expressed across this verse and the next. Philippians joins prayerful reliance upon God with His peace guarding hearts and thoughts. Both associate Godward reliance with peace; Isaiah's people keeping peace are not silently rewritten as God guarding their minds.

Isaiah 26 says the people hoped forever in the great everlasting God. Isaiah 12 likewise confesses trust in God the Savior and freedom from fear because He is salvation. Both express reliance upon the Lord within a communal song of deliverance.

Isaiah 26 brings high dwellings and fortified cities down to the ground. Isaiah 25 has just brought the high refuge of a wall to the ground. Their repeated contrast between defensive height and humiliating descent links the song with the preceding judgment oracle.

Isaiah gives the meek and lowly feet that trample the fallen defenses described immediately before. Malachi promises those who fear God's name that they will trample the lawless as ashes beneath their feet. Both show the Lord's people participating in the downfall announced by divine judgment, with different objects underfoot.

Isaiah describes the devout person's way as straight and prepared. Hosea likewise calls the Lord's ways straight and distinguishes the righteous who walk in them from the impious who grow weak in them. Both use the straight path for the course of a life ordered toward God.

Isaiah joins the Lord's way of judgment with hope in His name and remembrance. The psalm similarly places the Lord's enduring name and memorial immediately beside His judgment of His people. The same cluster ties divine remembrance to confidence in His dealings with the community.

Isaiah describes the spirit rising toward God from night and calls His ordinances light. The psalmist likewise rises at midnight to give thanks for God's righteous judgments. Both connect seeking God during the night with attention to His righteous ordering of life.

Isaiah says the ungodly will not learn righteousness or practice truth. Jeremiah likewise indicts leaders who do not know God: they are skilled in evil but have not learned to do well. Both describe moral failure as a refusal or failure to learn the good rather than a lack of worldly ability.

Isaiah announces fire consuming the opponents after their failure to recognize the Lord's raised arm. Hebrews likewise warns of a fury of fire about to consume the adversaries. The close fire-and-opponents formulation presents divine judgment in both settings; Hebrews applies the warning in its own context of deliberate sin.

Isaiah addresses the Lord directly with the plea to give His people peace. The priestly blessing likewise asks the Lord to lift His face upon the people and give peace. The correspondence rests on the requested divine gift, not on replacing Isaiah's statement about recompense with wording about God doing all human works.

Isaiah confesses knowing no other besides the Lord and naming His name. Hosea likewise declares that Israel is to know no god except the Lord and that no other saves. The confession answers the same exclusive allegiance that Hosea states as God's claim upon His people.

Isaiah first says that physicians cannot raise the dead. Later in the same song the dead rise and tombs awaken under healing dew from God. Reading the statements together distinguishes the failure of human healing power from the life-giving divine action subsequently promised.

The prayer asks for calamity upon the earth's glorious people. Isaiah 2 likewise announces the Lord's day against the high and elevated, bringing human height down so that the Lord alone is exalted. Both confront earthly eminence with divine abasement rather than treating prominence as protection.

Isaiah remembers the Lord in affliction and recognizes His discipline. The psalm recounts people seeking God and remembering their helper and redeemer when He struck them. Both connect distress with renewed remembrance of God; the psalm's following warning about insincere hearts is not suppressed or applied automatically to Isaiah's speaker.

Isaiah compares the people's fearful condition to a woman crying in labor. Jesus likewise uses a woman's birth anguish when explaining His disciples' sorrow and coming joy. Both make labor pain a picture of communal suffering, while John's explicit promise of seeing Jesus supplies its distinct narrative setting.

Isaiah 26 says the people conceived, labored and produced the spirit of God's salvation upon the earth. Isaiah 66 likewise depicts Zion laboring and bearing her children, asking about a nation born at once. Both use completed childbirth to picture a collective outcome; the native phrase about salvation is retained.

Isaiah announces that the dead rise and those in tombs awaken. Jesus likewise says that those in tombs will hear His voice and come out to resurrection. Both expressly describe the dead emerging from burial, while John distinguishes resurrection of life from resurrection of judgment.

Isaiah describes dead people in the earth awakening and rejoicing under God's healing dew. Daniel likewise announces the rising of those sleeping in the earth, with everlasting life and shame among the outcomes. The shared awakening image makes this a direct resurrection parallel without erasing their differing descriptions of judgment.

Isaiah commands the people to enter inner rooms, shut their door and hide until the Lord's wrath passes. Exodus similarly forbids leaving the house until morning as the Lord passes through to strike Egypt and protects the marked doorways. Both locate temporary refuge inside while destructive judgment passes outside.

relationship: blood and the earth as witness
rationale: Isaiah says the earth will uncover its blood and no longer cover those killed when the Lord brings wrath. Genesis gives Abel's blood a voice crying to God from the earth after his murder. Both deny that bloodshed hidden in the ground can escape divine acknowledgment.

Isaiah promises that the earth will uncover blood and cease concealing the slain. Job appeals directly to the earth not to cover his flesh's blood. Both give exposed blood the function of testimony, one as a prophetic announcement and the other as a sufferer's plea.

Isaiah announces God's killing the dragon with His great strong sword. The psalm likewise celebrates God's crushing the heads of dragons upon the water and the dragon's heads. Both use the defeat of a formidable dragon to portray divine power; no further identification of the creature is required by the comparison.

Isaiah's sword judgment targets the fleeing and crooked serpent described as a dragon. Job likewise credits God with killing the rebellious dragon by command. The shared decisive divine victory is explicit, although the dragon's descriptors and the means pictured differ.

Isaiah 27 introduces a beautiful vineyard and a song against her. Isaiah 5 likewise opens a vineyard song, then turns its cultivation story into a charge against Israel's failed righteousness. Both use the vineyard-song form for a communal address with judgment in its context, rather than presuming an uncomplicated celebration of a guarded vineyard.

Following the vineyard-song introduction, Isaiah 27 places a besieged city, watering in vain, night capture and a falling wall together. Isaiah 5 likewise removes the vineyard's fence and wall, leaving it trampled and without rain. Both depict failed protection in a vineyard oracle; the native watering in vain is not replaced by continual safe watering.

relationship: peace sought and granted after affliction
rationale: Isaiah 27's residents cry to make peace with Him amid the preceding burning and rejection. Isaiah 57 answers an earlier account of divine discipline with healing, comfort and peace upon peace. Both place restored peace in relation to the Lord after affliction, one as the residents' plea and the other as divine assurance.

Isaiah promises that Jacob's children and Israel will sprout, flower and fill the inhabited world with fruit. Hosea likewise promises Israel blossom, roots, spreading branches and the fruitfulness of olive and vine. Both describe the people's renewal through flourishing plants rather than through military expansion.

relationship: verbal correspondence in removal of sin
rationale: Isaiah links removal of Jacob's lawlessness with God's declaration about removing his sin. Romans likewise names the turning away of ungodliness from Jacob and concludes its written citation with God taking away their sins. The shared wording concerns Jacob's purification; Isaiah's word blessing and Romans' word covenant are preserved distinctly.

relationship: narrative illustration of destroyed cult objects
rationale: Isaiah joins removal of Jacob's sin with altar stones reduced to fine dust and the cutting down of trees and idols. Kings recounts Josiah shattering pillars, destroying groves and reducing Bethel's altar stones to dust. The acts give a concrete narrative counterpart to the dismantling of illicit worship described by Isaiah.

Isaiah 27 describes a released, abandoned flock with prolonged pasture and rest. Isaiah 17 describes an abandoned city becoming a resting place for flocks. Both bring flock, abandonment and rest together within judgment oracles; the native flock wording in Isaiah 27 is not silently rewritten as a fortified city.

Isaiah 27 explains the Maker's refusal of pity by the people's lack of understanding. Isaiah 1 likewise says Israel does not know and the people do not understand, then names their abandonment and provocation of the Lord. Both connect failure to recognize the One who formed or raised them with the ensuing indictment.

Isaiah marks the Lord's boundary from the River's canal to Rhinocorura and calls for Israel's sons to be gathered one by one. Deuteronomy promises God's gathering of Israel from even the remotest dispersion. Both envision the scattered people collected again; Isaiah's command and exact place name remain distinct from Deuteronomy's promise.

Isaiah 27 brings the lost from Assyria's country and Egypt to worship at Jerusalem. Isaiah 11 likewise names Assyria and Egypt among the places from which the Lord gathers His remaining people and the scattered of Israel. The repeated locations and gathering of the dispersed make the connection specific.

Isaiah sounds the great trumpet as dispersed people come to worship the Lord at Jerusalem. Matthew likewise joins a great trumpet with the gathering of the chosen from the four winds. The shared trumpet-and-gathering pattern is explicit, while Matthew's angels and Isaiah's named countries retain their different settings.
